value.overview: The Agami Heron (Agamia agami) is a striking, secretive heron of tropical Central and South America. It has a dark blue-green back, chestnut underparts, a long narrow bill, and pale blue facial markings. Unlike many conspicuous herons, it usually stays in dense vegetation along forest streams, swamps, lagoons, and mangroves. The species often nests in small colonies and is difficult to observe because it tends to forage quietly in shaded wetlands.
value.classification: The Agami Heron belongs to the heron family Ardeidae and is the only living species in the genus Agamia. It is sometimes called the Chestnut-bellied Heron.
value.identification: Adults are medium-sized herons with a long, pointed bill, elongated neck, and relatively short legs. The crown and upperparts are dark greenish blue, while the neck and body are rich chestnut, with pale blue skin around the eye and throat. Breeding birds may show elongated plumes on the head and neck. Juveniles are duller and browner. Its combination of deep chestnut underparts, dark upperparts, and secretive forest-wetland habits helps distinguish it from other Central American herons.
value.rangeHabitat: The Agami Heron ranges from eastern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America to the Amazon Basin. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon resident of lowland wet forests and wetlands, especially on the Caribbean slope and around the Golfo Dulce and Osa Peninsula, generally near rivers, lagoons, flooded forest, and mangroves. It favors quiet, densely vegetated freshwater or brackish habitats, usually from near sea level into the low foothills.
value.migrationStatus: The species is generally considered resident, including in Costa Rica. Clear long-distance migration is not established, but local or regional movements may occur, particularly after breeding or during seasonal changes in water conditions.
value.breeding: Agami Herons breed colonially, often in small, secluded rookeries in flooded forest, mangroves, or vegetation beside wetlands. They may nest near other waterbirds, including other herons and ibises. In Costa Rica, breeding has been documented, including colonies in the Caribbean lowlands, and more recent observations indicate that additional nesting sites may occur in suitable wetlands. Both adults contribute to nest building, incubation, and care of the young. Colonies are vulnerable to disturbance because suitable nesting habitat is limited.
value.dietFeeding: The Agami Heron mainly eats small fish, but also takes crustaceans, frogs, aquatic insects, and other small wetland animals. It usually forages alone in shallow water or along muddy banks, often beneath dense vegetation. The bird may stand motionless before making a quick thrust with its long bill. Its narrow body and long neck allow it to move through tangled vegetation and hunt along shaded forest streams.
value.behavior: This heron is notably secretive and is more often heard or glimpsed than seen clearly. It commonly moves slowly and deliberately through shadowed vegetation, keeping its body low while foraging. Individuals may perch quietly in trees or dense shrubs near water. Agami Herons are usually solitary outside the breeding season, but can gather at nesting colonies. Their quiet habits and preference for remote wetlands make population monitoring difficult.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although its total population size and detailed regional trends are not well known because the species is difficult to survey.
conservation.threats: Major concerns include the loss, degradation, and fragmentation of lowland wet forests, flooded forests, mangroves, and other wetlands. Drainage, agricultural conversion, logging, development, pollution, and disturbance at breeding colonies can reduce feeding and nesting habitat. Because Agami Herons often nest in small colonies, damage or repeated disturbance at a single rookery may affect many birds.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore lowland rivers, wetlands, mangroves, and forested waterways in Costa Rica and throughout the species’ range. Keep known nesting colonies undisturbed, especially during the breeding season, and support protected areas that include both feeding and roosting sites. Avoid clearing streamside vegetation, reduce pollution and pesticide runoff, and report sightings of colonies to local conservation authorities or bird-monitoring programs.
